title: Governance, Policy and Regulation

thumbnail.headline: Who Sets the AI Rules?
thumbnail.image: Navy background, a one-page policy document with three teal ticks beside a clean road-sign icon, a diverse staff meeting in the lower corner, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Who Sets the AI Rules?
slide.body: A one-page policy icon with three ticks: Rules · Oversight · Owners. Small tag: AI Literacy for Leaders · Lesson 7.

production_notes: [REGION] AI, data protection and professional rules differ by country and change often. The script names no specific laws and teaches questions for the legal team instead. A reviewer may add sourced regional notes after checking them.
[VERSION] Free plans of Claude and ChatGPT may have different data-use terms from business plans. Confirm current terms before recording, and keep the CTA reminder not to paste confidential data.
Kwame Asante and his accountancy firm in Ghana are fictional. Stock footage must not show a real firm name or logo.

Hook.voiceover: Some of your staff probably already use AI tools at work, with or without permission. So the question is not whether AI is in your organisation. The question is whether anyone has set the rules.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, we named the risks. Now let's set the rules that control them. AI governance is the set of rules, roles and reviews that keep AI use safe and in line with your goals. For most teams, it rests on three elements.

slide.title: Governance, Policy and Regulation
slide.body: Three pillars holding a roof labelled 'AI governance': 1. Rules for staff use · 2. Human oversight · 3. A named owner per system.

Explain.voiceover: The first is clear rules for staff use of AI tools. An acceptable-use policy says which tools are approved, what data people may enter, and when they must check AI output. It also asks people to report anything harmful or clearly wrong. Keep it short, practical and in plain language.

slide.title: 1. An acceptable-use policy
slide.body: Use only approved tools and accounts · No personal, client or confidential data in unapproved tools · A person checks AI output before it leaves the organisation · Report harmful or wrong output.

Explain.voiceover: The second is human oversight for important decisions. Decisions that affect people's jobs, money, health, rights or access to services need a named person who reviews the AI's suggestion and can change it. The more serious the impact, the stronger the review.

slide.title: 2. Human oversight
slide.body: A dial from 'Low impact' to 'High impact: jobs, money, health, rights, services'. As the dial rises, the review box grows stronger. A person icon with a pen: can change the AI's suggestion.

Explain.voiceover: The third is a named owner for each AI system. The owner knows what the tool does, what data it uses, how it performs and when to review it. A simple list of your AI systems and their owners is one of the most useful governance tools you can create.

slide.title: 3. A named owner per system
slide.body: Simple table: AI system | What it does | Data used | Owner | Next review. Three example rows with role titles, not names.

Explain.voiceover: What about regulation? AI and data protection rules differ between countries, and they are changing. You do not need to memorise laws. You need to ask your legal team the right questions. Which rules apply where we operate? Does this use involve personal data? Does it affect decisions about people? What do our contracts say? And what must we document?

slide.title: Questions for your legal team
slide.body: Which laws and sector rules apply in each country? · Personal data involved, and a legal basis? · Decisions about people needing extra controls? · What do client and vendor contracts say? · What must we document, and for how long?

Explain.voiceover: Think of the rules of the road. Traffic rules do not stop people from driving. They make it safe for many people to drive at the same time. A clear AI policy lets staff use AI with confidence, instead of guessing or hiding it.
Explain.stock_query: busy city intersection traffic flowing smoothly
Explain.on_screen_text: Rules make it safe to drive

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see governance in practice. Kwame Asante is managing partner of a fictional accountancy firm in Ghana, with forty-five staff. He learns that several staff use free AI chat tools to draft client letters. One has pasted a client's financial figures into a tool. This is exactly the privacy risk we saw in the last lesson.
Demonstrate.stock_query: accountants working at desks in office

Demonstrate.voiceover: Kwame does not ban AI. He asks an AI assistant to draft a one-page policy, using only a general description of the firm. The draft is useful, but too general. So he edits it.

slide.title: From general draft to firm policy
slide.body: Left: AI draft, generic rules, greyed out. Right: Kwame's edits appear one by one in the next scene.

Demonstrate.voiceover: He names one approved business account for client data, after his IT provider checks its data terms. Every client letter drafted with AI must be checked and signed by a qualified accountant. The operations manager owns the list of AI tools. And he asks the firm's legal adviser which rules apply to client data in AI tools.

slide.title: Kwame's edits
slide.body: One approved business account for client data, after IT checks terms · Every AI-drafted client letter checked and signed by a qualified accountant · Owner of AI tool list: operations manager · Legal question: which rules apply to client data in AI tools?

Demonstrate.voiceover: He shares the policy in a staff meeting, explains the reasons behind each rule and invites questions. Staff say they feel more confident, because they now know what is allowed.
Demonstrate.stock_query: managing partner leading friendly staff meeting

Demonstrate.voiceover: This avoids a common mistake: the total ban. Bans are hard to enforce, and staff often keep using personal accounts where you have no control. A clear policy with approved tools usually reduces risk more than a ban does. Kwame turned hidden use into safe, visible use.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: A clear policy beats a ban

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, good AI governance rests on clear rules for staff, human oversight for important decisions, and a named owner for each AI system. Second, an acceptable-use policy should be short, practical and specific about which data may go into which tools. Third, laws differ and change, so ask your legal team the right questions.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Governance = staff rules · human oversight · named owners. 2. Policy: short, practical, specific about data. 3. Laws differ and change: ask your legal team the right questions.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will use Claude or ChatGPT to draft a one-page acceptable-use policy for your team. Use general terms only, with no confidential information. Then edit every rule so it fits your organisation, and add three questions for your legal team. In the next lesson, we cover asking vendors the right questions. See you there.
